chapter: Reel 3: defining jazz and the blues
title: Bernstein's praise and why the blues may not be jazz
summary: Leonard Bernstein called his blues the greatest ever; Johnson says the blues is the poor man's feelings and asks what jazz is.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: All right. Let's go to the blues.
You told me the last time we talked that the blues wasn't really jazz; yet, you know what Leonard Bernstein said -- that you wrote the greatest blues jazz piece ever written, the most perfect one.
Well, that's a literal expression, that's a personal thing. I mean, he carried it throughout his book, you know, he wrote a book about it and he carried that throughout his book, so ...
But Leonard Bernstein is a genius anyway; he's my idea of a -- well, you just don't top him. He's up there where it is.
We have out J.C. Johnson Festival and Jazz Tribute -- he's one of the people he's on our list to
invite, and I'll bet you anything he's going to show up. But let's get now down to the blues. How would you define the blues?
Well, the blues -- I'd define it in the books, Scott has it there.
Do you want to get that, Scott? That's J.C.'s book of poetry. Right. Do you want me to find it?
All right. The last time we were talking, you said the blues was the poor man's feelings.
But why are you so -- I would almost say persistent about saying the blues, in your opinion, really isn't jazz.
